---
title: "How CVD deaths are classified"
description: "How BNR uses death-certificate information to create practical cardiovascular mortality classifications."
---

BNR uses a practical classification method to identify deaths with evidence of cardiovascular disease when a formally assigned national underlying cause of death is not available to the Registry for routine surveillance.

## Why this matters

A death certificate can mention several diseases and conditions. A cardiovascular term appearing anywhere on the certificate does not automatically mean that cardiovascular disease should be treated as the underlying cause.

BNR therefore uses a structured method that considers:

- the wording recorded on the death certificate;
- whether information appears in Part I or Part II;
- the order of the lines in Part I;
- a small number of documented mortality-coding principles; and
- the strength and uncertainty of the available evidence.

The aim is a consistent **approximate cardiovascular mortality classification**, not a replacement for formal national cause-of-death coding.

## Evidence classes

The classifier places cardiovascular evidence into five broad classes.

| Class | Plain-English meaning |
|---|---|
| **Clear** | Strong evidence that the death belongs in the relevant BNR cardiovascular mortality group |
| **Likely** | Good evidence, although some uncertainty remains |
| **Possible** | A cardiovascular attribution is plausible, but uncertainty is material |
| **Mention only** | Relevant wording is present but does not support approximate underlying-cause attribution |
| **No evidence** | No qualifying evidence was identified by the approved rules |

## The two public definitions

The mortality dashboard uses two nested definitions.

| Definition | Evidence included |
|---|---|
| **Primary** | Clear + Likely |
| **Inclusive** | Clear + Likely + Possible |

The Inclusive definition is deliberately broader. Comparing the two gives readers a simple indication of how much the reported burden changes when more uncertain cardiovascular deaths are included.

These are **classification-sensitivity definitions**, not confidence intervals and not statistical lower and upper bounds.

## Heart and Stroke

BNR mortality reporting distinguishes two broad cardiovascular families.

**Heart** includes compatible ischaemic and coronary heart disease evidence. It is not limited to certificates that literally use the words acute myocardial infarction or heart attack.

**Stroke** includes qualifying acute ischaemic stroke and non-traumatic cerebral haemorrhage patterns within the approved BNR Stroke family. Explicit traumatic and other excluded haemorrhage patterns are not treated as direct Stroke evidence under these rules.

The public dashboard also reports **All CVD**, combining the resolved Heart and Stroke classifications according to the approved mortality method.

## What happens when the certificate structure is uncertain?

The position of information on the death certificate matters. If the original causal line structure is uncertain or has been combined in a way that loses that ordering, the classifier does not simply assume the strongest evidence class.

This is one reason BNR retains explicit uncertainty classes rather than forcing every cardiovascular mention into a single yes/no category.

## This is not full ICD-10 underlying-cause coding

The BNR method uses some mortality-coding principles, but it does not implement the full international process for selecting and coding an official underlying cause of death.

It should therefore not be described as equivalent to formal ICD-10 underlying-cause coding or to automated mortality-coding systems used for official national statistics.

::: {.callout-warning title="Compare mortality series carefully"}
An official national or international CVD mortality series may use different source information, ICD-10 code selections and underlying-cause rules. Similar labels do not guarantee equivalent definitions.
:::

## What to remember

- A cardiovascular mention is not automatically classified as a cardiovascular underlying cause.
- Primary includes Clear and Likely evidence.
- Inclusive adds Possible evidence.
- Inclusive contains Primary, so the two definitions must not be added together.
- The method is designed for consistent BNR surveillance, not as a substitute for formal national cause-of-death coding.
